learningPath.title: Connected Learning
learningPath.description: The connected learning path. Competencies demonstrated in one course are reused by later courses rather than duplicated.

course.title: Networking Foundations
course.description: Start from nothing and build a working mental model of how two machines reach each other. You will meet the devices a network is made of, watch traffic move inside one network, learn the two identities a machine carries, work out the decision every machine makes about where to send something, follow a message across a boundary and back, test whether it truly arrived, and repair a simple failure. Before this course you need only the ability to operate a computer, use a keyboard and mouse, navigate a web application, and compare two numbers. No networking vocabulary is assumed: every term you need is introduced here, after you have already seen the behaviour it names.

modules.title: One Network
modules.description: What a network is made of, and how something gets from one machine to another when both are on the same network. Everything here happens inside a single network; boundaries come later.

modules.title: Addresses and Boundaries
modules.description: The second identity a machine carries, and the decision it makes with it: is what I am trying to reach on my own network, or somewhere else? This is the question the rest of the course depends on.

modules.title: Reaching Another Network
modules.description: What a machine does when the answer is "somewhere else": who it hands the message to, what that device does with it, and what the whole trip looks like from one end to the other.

modules.title: Prove It and Fix It
modules.description: Establishing whether something genuinely works rather than appears to, and what to do when it does not. The failure here is bounded and visible; finding a fault you were not shown belongs to a later course.

missions.title: Mission 1 — Follow something across a network
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: operate a computer, and compare two numbers. Nothing else.

When you print a document on a network printer, your computer has to get the print request from where you are sitting to the printer itself. In this mission you follow that request across a small network and see which devices it passes through.

First you meet the devices a small network is made of: the machines people use, the device in the middle that connects them, and the device at the edge that connects this network to other networks. You see where each one sits and what it is attached to.

Then you follow one print request from the computer that sent it to the printer that produces it, predicting where it goes before you watch it happen.

This mission does not teach how the device in the middle makes its decision, and it does not teach what the device at the edge does. Both are deliberate. You will finish with two specific questions, and the missions that follow answer them.

Nothing is configured or changed here. You are learning to read a network before you are asked to alter one.

content.title: Follow something across a network
paragraphs: When you print a document on a network printer, your computer has to get the print request from where you are sitting to the printer itself. The request does not arrive there by magic. It travels, and it passes through other devices on the way.
In this mission you follow one print request across a small network and see which devices it passes through.

You will learn what a network is at a basic level, what a host is, what a network connection represents, where a switch sits in a small network, and how to follow information from one device to another.
You will configure nothing and change nothing. You are learning to read a network before you are asked to alter one.

content.title: What is a host?
paragraphs: Computers on a network are often called hosts. A desktop, a laptop or a server connected to a network can be a host, and so is the phone in your pocket.
A host is where information starts, or where it finishes. PC-A and PC-B are hosts in the network you are about to see.

A printer connected to the network is a host too. The diagrams in this course label a printer as a printer so that you can recognise it at a glance, but for the purpose of getting information from one place to another, it behaves exactly as a computer does.

content.title: Network connections
paragraphs: Devices communicate through network connections. A host does not join a network by being near it: every host has a specific place where the connection arrives — the socket at the back of a laptop, the aerial inside a phone. That connection point is called an interface.
A device built to hold many connections usually calls each one a port rather than an interface. Port and interface name the same idea, and this course uses whichever word the device itself would use.
The connection running between two interfaces is called a link. PC-A has one link, so everything PC-A puts onto this network leaves the same way, and that link is its way in.

content.title: The device in the middle, and the device at the edge
paragraphs: Not every device on a network is a host. A small network also contains devices whose only job is to carry traffic between the hosts, and you can tell them apart by what each one is attached to.

One device sits in the middle. Every host has one link, and every one of those links ends at this same device, each host on a port of its own. No host has a link to another host, so anything travelling between two hosts passes through the device in the middle. That device is called a switch, and this one is named Switch-1.

One device sits at the edge. It is attached to Switch-1, and it is also attached to a connection that leads out of this network entirely. That second attachment is what makes it a different kind of device. It is called a router, and this one is named Router-1.

We will not use Router-1 in this mission. It is here so that you can recognise a router and see where one sits, because Router-1 marks the point where this local network stops. You will discover why it is there in a later mission.

content.caption: Follow the print request. Someone at PC-A wants to print a document using the network printer, so PC-A sends a print request. Follow it from PC-A to the Printer. Select any device to read what it is and what it connects to.
content.textEquivalent: A small network of five devices. Three of them are hosts: PC-A and PC-B are computers people use, and the Printer is the network printer. Each host has one network interface and one link, and every one of those links runs to Switch-1 — PC-A to port 1, PC-B to port 2, the Printer to port 3. Switch-1 is the device in the middle: Switch-1 holds four ports, and every local connection in this network arrives at one of them. Router-1 is attached to Switch-1 on port 4 through its local port, and Router-1 also has a second, outward port whose connection leads away from this network entirely. No link joins two hosts directly, so any path between two hosts runs through Switch-1. Someone at PC-A wants to print a document, so PC-A sends a print request towards the Printer. You are asked to predict which device the print request reaches first. The print request leaves PC-A along PC-A's single link and arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 then passes it on, and the print request arrives at the Printer over the link that ends on Switch-1 port 3, where the Printer accepts the print job. The walkthrough is then complete. PC-B and Router-1 receive nothing and are not visited. How Switch-1 works out which port leads to the Printer is Mission 2, and what Router-1 does is Mission 5 and Mission 6. You can select any device at any point to read what it is, which interfaces it has, and what it connects to.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the computer a person is working at, and it is where this print request begins. It has one network connection, and that connection runs to Switch-1.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is a second computer on this local network, connected to Switch-1 the same way PC-A is. It is here because a network is shared: several machines connect to the same switch, each on a connection of its own. This print request came from PC-A, so PC-B plays no part in it.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is the shared network printer, and it is what this print request is for. It is a host like PC-A and PC-B, with a connection into Switch-1 of its own, which is what lets any computer on this network send it work.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 is the device in the middle of this local network. PC-A, PC-B, the Printer and Router-1 each connect to a port on it, so anything one of them sends arrives at Switch-1 first. Mission 2 explains how Switch-1 decides which port to send it out of.

nodes.label: Router-1
nodes.about: Router-1 sits at the edge of this local network, with one port facing Switch-1 and one port leading away. It is the way out when a machine here needs to reach something that is not on this network. This print request does not use Router-1, because PC-A and the Printer are both on this local network. Mission 5 explains why a computer sends traffic to a router when what it wants is somewhere else.

stages.narration: The print request leaves PC-A along PC-A's single link.
stages.decision: PC-A is the computer sending the print request. It has one link, so everything PC-A sends leaves the same way.

prediction.prompt: PC-A sends the print request towards the Printer. Which device does the print request reach first?

stages.narration: The print request arrives at Switch-1, on port 1.
stages.decision: PC-A's link ends at port 1 on Switch-1, so Switch-1 is the first device the print request reaches. But the print request is meant for the Printer, so what does Switch-1 do with it? That is what Mission 2 begins investigating; continue to see where the print request goes.

stages.narration: The print request arrives at the Printer, and the Printer accepts the print job.
stages.decision: The Printer connects to Switch-1 on port 3, and that link carried the print request the rest of the way. The document a user asked for at PC-A has reached the machine that will produce it.

confirmation.narration: The print request reached the network printer, and the printer accepted the print job.
confirmation.summary: PC-A sent it, Switch-1 was in the middle, and the Printer received it. You have followed one print request from the machine that sent it to the machine it was for. Now you may be wondering how Switch-1 knew where to send it, and why the print request did not go through Router-1. Those are the right questions to be left with: Mission 2 answers the first, and Missions 5 and 6 answer the second.

content.title: Reading the picture
paragraphs: The drawing you just worked through has a name. A picture of what is connected to what is called a topology.

A topology is not a floor plan. Two devices drawn beside each other may sit in different rooms, and a line drawn between them may be a cable running through three walls. A topology shows relationships, not distances, and reading a topology as a map of the building is the most common way to misread one.

You can now do something that every mission after this one depends on: look at a small network, say what each device is for, name the link between any two devices, and say which device a message must pass through to get from one host to another.

missions.title: Mission 2 — Inside one network: how a switch delivers
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a small network and name its devices and connections (Mission 1).

Two machines are connected to the same device in the middle. Someone at one of them sends a file to a colleague at the other. Watch what happens the first time, and then watch what happens the second time. They are not the same, and the difference is the whole of this mission.

The first time, the device in the middle does not know where the destination is, so it sends a copy of the file out of every other connection at once and lets the right machine answer. That is wasteful, and it does not stay that way. The device pays attention to which connection each delivery arrives on, records what it observes, and the next one goes to exactly one place.

Once you have seen that happen, you get the words for it. Each machine carries a built-in identity set at the factory, written in a notation you will recognise but do not need to calculate with. The unit of traffic that carries one of these identities to another has a name. The record the middle device builds up has a name. Sending a copy to everyone because you do not yet know better has a name too.

You will also meet the first thing that looks like a failure and is not. Traffic reaching every machine instead of one looks wrong the first time you see it. It is correct, it is temporary, and telling the difference between "broken" and "working as designed" is a habit worth forming early.

By the end you will be able to explain how one machine reaches another inside a single network, why the second attempt behaves differently from the first, and what happens when the destination is not known.

content.title: One file, two machines
paragraphs: Someone at PC-A is sharing a file with a colleague at PC-B. PC-A and PC-B are on the same small network, each with a link into Switch-1, and no other device stands between them.
PC-A addresses the file to PC-B's interface. PC-A can do that because it already holds an identity for that interface — a value naming which connection point on the network the file is for.

How PC-A came to hold that identity is a real question with a real answer, and the answer needs one idea you do not have yet. The question is not being waved away: Mission 4 answers it. For now, take it as given that PC-A knows which interface it is addressing, and watch what the network does with the file.
You will watch this twice. The same file is sent to the same machine on two separate occasions, and the two occasions do not go the same way. The difference between them is the whole of this mission.

content.caption: An instructional walkthrough of two deliveries on one network. This is authored teaching, not a live environment, and nothing here is running on real hardware.
content.textEquivalent: A small network of four devices: three hosts — PC-A, PC-B and a Printer — each with one interface, and Switch-1 in the middle holding three ports. PC-A is on port 1, PC-B on port 2, the Printer on port 3. Each host interface carries a hardware identity, which you can read in the inspector. Someone at PC-A is sending a file to a colleague at PC-B, and the walkthrough follows that file being sent twice. The first time, PC-A puts the file onto its connection addressed to PC-B, and it arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 holds no record of where PC-B is, so at that same moment it sends a copy of the file out of both of its other connections at once — port 2 and port 3. These are two copies of one delivery, not two separate files. The copy on port 2 reaches PC-B, which is the machine the file is addressed to, and PC-B accepts it. The copy on port 3 reaches the Printer, which compares the file's destination against its own identity, sees that they are different, and does not accept it; nothing has gone wrong there. As the file arrived, Switch-1 recorded what it could see: the file came in on port 1 from PC-A, so PC-A is on port 1. Switch-1 still has no record of PC-B. PC-B then replies, and that reply arrives at Switch-1 on port 2, which is how Switch-1 records that PC-B is on port 2. The reply leaves by port 1 alone and reaches PC-A, because Switch-1 already knew where PC-A was. The second time, PC-A sends the same file to PC-B again and nothing about the file has changed. Switch-1 receives it on port 1, finds PC-B already recorded against port 2, and sends it out of port 2 only. Port 3 stays quiet and the Printer sees nothing at all. The file reaches PC-B. What changed between the two deliveries is not the file: it is what Switch-1 had recorded from the ordinary traffic it saw in between.

nodes.label: PC-A
nodes.about: PC-A is the computer sending the file, in both of the deliveries this walkthrough follows. It connects to port 1 on Switch-1, and it addresses the file to PC-B's interface.

nodes.label: PC-B
nodes.about: PC-B is the machine the file is meant for, both times it is sent. It connects to port 2 on Switch-1, and its interface carries the hardware identity PC-A addresses the file to.

nodes.label: Printer
nodes.about: The Printer is a third host on this network, connected to port 3. The file is not meant for it either time. Watch what reaches the Printer during the first delivery and what does not reach it during the second, because the difference between those two moments is the whole of this mission.

nodes.label: Switch-1
nodes.about: Switch-1 connects all three hosts, one to each port. Everything in this walkthrough arrives here first, and what Switch-1 does with it changes between the first delivery and the second. What it records in between is the subject of this mission.

stages.narration: The person at PC-A shares a file with a colleague at PC-B. PC-A puts the file onto its connection, addressed to PC-B.
stages.decision: PC-A does not decide how the file will travel. PC-A addresses it and sends it; working out which connection leads where is not PC-A's job.

stages.narration: The file arrives at Switch-1 on port 1. Switch-1 holds no record of where PC-B is, so at that same moment it sends a copy of the file out of both of its other connections at once — port 2 and port 3. These are two copies of one delivery, not two separate files.
stages.decision: Switch-1 is not guessing and it is not giving up. It has one delivery for PC-B and no record of which connection leads there, so it uses every connection it has left. Whichever one PC-B is on, the file arrives.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has only just been switched on. Nothing addressed to PC-B has ever passed through it. What does Switch-1 do with this file?
options: Sends it out of port 2 only, because that is where PC-B is
Sends a copy out of every other connection, because it does not yet know which one leads to PC-B
Holds on to it and asks PC-B where it is

stages.narration: The copy on port 2 reaches PC-B, which is the machine the file is addressed to, so PC-B accepts it. The copy on port 3 reaches the Printer at the same moment. The Printer compares the file's destination against its own identity, sees that they are different, and does not accept it.
stages.decision: Nothing has gone wrong at the Printer. Every machine checks whether an arriving delivery is addressed to it, and leaves it alone when it is not. Meanwhile Switch-1 recorded what it could see as the file came past: the file arrived on port 1 and PC-A sent it, so PC-A is on port 1. Nobody configured that. Switch-1 still has no record of PC-B, because PC-B has not sent anything yet.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has now seen the file arrive from PC-A on port 1. What does Switch-1 know at this point?
options: Both where PC-A is and where PC-B is

facts.label: Copy arrived
facts.value: Not accepted — the file is addressed to PC-B

stages.narration: PC-B answers, and its reply arrives at Switch-1 on port 2.
stages.decision: Switch-1 records this arrival exactly as it recorded the first one: the reply came in on port 2 and PC-B sent it, so PC-B is on port 2. That is the one thing Switch-1 was missing a moment ago, and ordinary traffic supplied it.

stages.narration: The reply leaves by port 1 alone and arrives at PC-A. The Printer's connection stays quiet this time.
stages.decision: Switch-1 already knew that PC-A was on port 1, because it recorded that when the file first came past. The reply therefore never needed to go anywhere else.

stages.narration: A little later, the person at PC-A sends the same file to PC-B again. Nothing about the file itself has changed.
stages.decision: Same sender, same destination, same network, same file. The only thing that is different is what has happened in between.

stages.narration: The file arrives at Switch-1 on port 1 again. This time Switch-1 finds PC-B already recorded against port 2, and sends the file out of port 2 alone. Port 3 stays quiet, and the Printer sees nothing at all.
stages.decision: This is the whole difference. Switch-1 is no cleverer than it was a minute ago. It simply knows one thing now that it did not know then, and it learned that thing by watching ordinary traffic that nobody sent for the purpose.

prediction.prompt: Switch-1 has now seen a reply arrive from PC-B on port 2. What does it do with this second copy of the file?
options: Sends a copy out of every other connection again
Sends it out of port 2 only
Waits for PC-B to answer before sending anything

stages.narration: The file arrives at PC-B. One copy, one connection, and nothing anywhere else on the network.
stages.decision: Compare that with the first delivery: the same two machines and the same file, but one connection used instead of three.

confirmation.narration: The file reached PC-B directly the second time, and the Printer never saw it.
confirmation.summary: The first time, Switch-1 had no record of where PC-B was, so it sent a copy of the file out of every other connection at once and the file still arrived. Switch-1 recorded where each machine was by watching ordinary traffic arrive — PC-A when the file came past, PC-B when the reply came back. By the second time Switch-1 knew, so one copy out of one connection was enough.

content.title: What you just watched
paragraphs: The first time, Switch-1 had never seen anything addressed to PC-B, so Switch-1 did not know which of its ports led there. Switch-1 did the one thing that reliably works: at the same moment, it sent a copy out of every other connection, so that whichever one led to PC-B, the file would arrive. Sending a copy out of the other connections because the destination has not been learned yet is called flooding.

Flooding is not a failure and not a mistake. Flooding is what a switch does when it does not yet know where a destination is, and it succeeds — the file reached PC-B. Flooding is merely wasteful, because the Printer was handed a copy it had no use for.

Flooding also does not last. Everything arriving at a switch shows which port it came in on and which interface sent it, and a switch keeps a record of what it sees. Switch-1 recorded PC-A against port 1 the instant the file first came past, and PC-B against port 2 the instant PC-B's reply arrived. Switch-1 builds that record out of ordinary traffic, and nobody configures it.

Notice the order. Switch-1 learned where the SENDER was from the very first delivery, because the sender is the one thing an arriving delivery always shows. It could not learn where PC-B was until PC-B sent something of its own — which is why the record had one entry after the first delivery and two after the reply.

By the second delivery Switch-1 had PC-B on that record, so there was nothing to work out: one connection, one copy, and the Printer's connection left quiet. Nothing about the file changed between the two deliveries. What changed is what Switch-1 knew.

content.title: The identity on an interface
paragraphs: The value you could read on each interface in the inspector is the identity PC-A addressed the file to, and the same value is what Switch-1 recorded against a port. That value is called a MAC address.

A MAC address belongs to an interface rather than to a machine, so a laptop with both a socket and an aerial carries two MAC addresses. A MAC address is set when the hardware is made rather than chosen afterwards, and for delivery within one local network it is the identity that matters.

You read a MAC address. You do not calculate with it. A MAC address is written as six pairs of characters separated by colons, and for now that is the whole of what you need to know about the notation.

The record you watched Switch-1 build has a name as well: it is the MAC address table. The walkthrough showed it with device names — PC-A, PC-B — so that you could read it at a glance before you had met the term. What a switch actually stores against each port is the MAC address of the interface it last saw sending there. Same record, same behaviour, written the way the switch holds it.

content.caption: The MAC address of one interface, as a real machine reports it. This is displayed output for you to read — nothing here offers to run anything. Real output carries several more lines and several more fields; this shows only the line that matters here, so that nothing appears which you have not met yet.

content.title: The unit that moved
paragraphs: Something specific travelled from PC-A's interface to a port on Switch-1, and then from a port on Switch-1 to PC-B's interface. That thing carried the address of the interface it was for, and the address of the interface that sent it.
That unit is called a frame. A frame is what moves across one local network, from interface to interface, addressed by the kind of address you have just met.

A second unit exists, with a different name and a different job, and it becomes important the moment something has to leave this network. Naming that second unit now would mean nothing to you, because you have not yet watched anything leave. You meet it in Mission 6, where the difference between the two finally has something to be a difference about.

content.title: Looks wrong, works as designed
paragraphs: The Printer was handed a copy of a file that had nothing to do with the Printer, compared the address on that copy against its own, saw that the two did not match, and did not accept it. Nothing went wrong.

The first time you see traffic arriving somewhere it was not meant for, it looks like a fault. Form the habit now of asking a different question first: is this broken, or is this the system working as designed?
You will need that question for the rest of this course. You will need it most in Mission 8, where something genuinely is broken and telling the difference is the entire job.

missions.title: Mission 3 — IPv4 addresses: the second identity
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: explain how one machine reaches another inside a single network, and what the built-in factory identity is for (Mission 2).

Every machine you have looked at already has an identity. So why does it need a second one?

The factory identity has a problem: it says nothing about where the machine is. It cannot be changed, it follows the hardware, and it is useless for organising anything. A second identity fixes that. It is assigned rather than built in, it is written as four numbers separated by dots, and unlike the first one it can be chosen to say something about which group a machine belongs to.

You will look at real output from a machine and find its second identity, sitting next to the name of the connection that holds it. Reading that output is a small skill with a large payoff: it is how you confirm what a machine actually has, rather than what someone told you it has.

This mission does not yet tell you how a machine uses the second identity to decide anything. That decision needs one more piece of information, and it is the whole of the next mission. Here you are establishing the fact that the identity exists, that it is assigned, that it can be read, and that it is a different kind of thing from the one you met in Mission 2.

Addresses can be set by hand or handed out automatically by another machine. This course sets them by hand so you can see exactly what is where. Machines can also be reached by name rather than by address; that is a separate system, and this course works in addresses deliberately.

By the end you will be able to read a machine's assigned address from real output, say which connection holds it, and explain how it differs from the identity you met in Mission 2. You will use that in every mission that follows, and in every later course that asks you to check what a machine actually has.

missions.title: Mission 4 — The prefix, and the decision every host makes
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: read a machine's assigned address from real output (Mission 3), and compare two numbers.

This is the mission the rest of the course rests on.

An assigned address is written with a second number after it. That number says how much of the address names the group the machine belongs to, and how much names the machine itself. A larger number means more of the address is fixed and the group is smaller. You will compare two of them so the number stops being decoration and starts being a quantity.

With that, a machine can answer the only question that matters before it sends anything: is what I am trying to reach part of my own group, or not? Watch a machine answer it both ways. When the answer is yes, it delivers directly, using what you learned in Mission 2 — and you will see the small exchange it performs first to turn an assigned address into the factory identity it actually needs to address the traffic. When the answer is no, it does something you have not seen before: it hands the traffic to a different device entirely, one it was not trying to reach.

That hand-off will look wrong. Nothing was delivered to the destination, and yet nothing is broken. Deciding whether what you are watching is a fault or correct behaviour is the most useful question in this course, and this is the first place you get to ask it with enough information to answer.

You will not be told what that other device is called yet. You will see what it receives and why, and the name comes next.

By the end you will be able to take two machines' addresses and say whether one will deliver to the other directly, and say what it does instead when it will not.

missions.title: Mission 5 — The default gateway
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: decide from two addresses whether a machine will deliver directly, and describe what it does instead when it will not (Mission 4).

In Mission 4 you watched a machine hand traffic to a device it was not trying to reach. That device has a name, and the machine did not guess at it — the address was configured in advance, and it is the machine's answer to "this is not for my group, so it is your problem now".

You will read that configuration from real output. There is one line in it that matters here, and you will learn to find that line and ignore the rest, which is a skill in itself.

Then you will work out why that address and not another. The device a machine hands traffic to has to be one the machine can reach directly, or the hand-off could never happen — which means it must be in the machine's own group. That single constraint explains almost every mistake people make with this setting, and you will meet one of those mistakes in Mission 8.

This is the smallest mission in the course, and deliberately so. It introduces one idea and one line of output. What that device actually does with the traffic once it has it is the next mission.

By the end you will be able to identify which address a machine will hand off to, and explain why that address has to be the one it is.

missions.title: Mission 6 — Routers, and the journey end to end
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: identify the device a machine hands off to and explain why it must be reachable directly (Mission 5).

Everything so far has been one half of a trip. Now you follow a whole one.

A message leaves a machine in one group, crosses to a device that belongs to two groups at once, and comes out the other side into a group it was never part of. Watch what changes at that device and what does not. The destination does not change — it was decided before the message left and it survives the whole trip. What wraps around it is thrown away and rebuilt at every step, because each step is a different local delivery of the kind you learned in Mission 2.

That distinction — the part that survives the journey and the part that is rebuilt for each leg — is the single most useful idea in this course, and it only makes sense once you have watched it happen. You have now watched local delivery twice and a hand-off once, so it is time.

Then the reply comes back, the same way in reverse, and you watch that too. A trip that only goes one way is not communication.

At the end of this mission, and not before, you get two labels. The decisions about reaching someone in your own group have a common name. The decisions about reaching another group have a different one. These are names for behaviour you have already understood, not a framework to memorise. There are formal models that number these layers; you will meet them when you have a reason to, and this course does not give you one.

This mission introduces no new responsibility of its own. It puts five missions together into one continuous story, which is why nothing new is developed here and everything is used.

missions.title: Mission 7 — Testing whether it actually works
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: follow a message from one group to another and back, and say what changes at each step (Mission 6).

So far you have been shown what happens. Now you find out for yourself.

There is a small test that asks a machine to answer, and reports whether it did. You will run it and read what comes back. Reading it is not the interesting part; deciding what to test is.

Here is the trap. A test that succeeds proves something specific, and it is almost never the thing people assume it proves. If a machine can reach the device it hands off to, that proves the first step works and says nothing about the rest of the trip. If it cannot reach that device, then nothing beyond it can possibly work, and testing anything further is wasted effort. Choosing what to test, in what order, so that each result actually narrows things down, is a different skill from running the test.

You will practise the difference between a result that confirms what you believe and a result that is merely consistent with it. Those feel identical in the moment and are not the same, and telling them apart is what separates someone who is checking from someone who is guessing.

By the end you will be able to choose which address to test in order to establish a specific claim, and say what a successful result does and does not prove.

missions.title: Mission 8 — When it does not work
missions.description:
Before this mission you should be able to: choose a test that establishes a specific claim, and say what its result proves (Mission 7).

Something is wrong, and this time it really is wrong.

A message leaves and does not arrive. You will watch where it stops. You are shown the stopping point in this mission — you are not yet being asked to find a failure nobody has located for you, which is a harder skill and belongs to a later course. What you are asked to do here is reason about what a visible stopping point tells you.

Work backwards from it. The last thing that behaved correctly tells you what is still intact. The first thing that did not tells you where to look. Everything you have built across seven missions is what makes that reasoning possible: you know what should have happened at each step, so you can tell which step did not do it.

The cause is a single wrong setting, of a kind you were warned about in Mission 5. Correct it, and then — this is the part that matters — watch the message go the whole way and the reply come back. A repair you did not confirm is not a repair; it is a hope. The confirmation is not a formality at the end of the mission, it is the point of it.

By the end you will have taken a bounded failure from symptom to evidence to correction to proof, which is the shape of every piece of troubleshooting you will ever do.

This mission develops no new responsibility. It is where everything the course built gets used at once, which is the only honest test of whether it was built properly.

competencies.title: Network topology literacy
competencies.description: Identify the hosts, switches and routers in a network topology, name the interfaces and ports that connect them, and state which device is responsible for each part of a path between two machines.

competencies.title: Local network delivery
competencies.description: Explain how a switch delivers traffic to one host within a single network, how it learns where hosts are, what it does with a destination it has not learned, and why traffic for another network is handed elsewhere.

competencies.title: IPv4 address identification
competencies.description: Identify the IPv4 address assigned to a host's interface, read it from device or operating-system output, and distinguish an assigned address from the interface's built-in hardware identity.

competencies.title: IPv4 addressing
competencies.description: Assign and interpret an IPv4 address and prefix length, and determine which addresses a host can reach without assistance from a router.

competencies.title: Subnet boundaries
competencies.description: Determine from an address and prefix length whether two hosts share a subnet, and recognise the boundary at which forwarding becomes a router's responsibility.

competencies.title: Default gateway relationships
competencies.description: Identify the correct default gateway for a host and explain why off-subnet traffic depends on it.

competencies.title: Connectivity verification
competencies.description: Choose verification steps that establish what actually works, and distinguish a test that confirms a hypothesis from one merely consistent with it.
